Sun Paper Art: A Macro-Scale Analogy

Before we dive back into the microscopic world, I wanted to show you what I made with the sun paper I handed out last time. You might remember I showed you a photomask with a “67” on it, and for good measure, I also tried to pattern the logo for my favorite sports team, the Los Angeles Dodgers. It sort of worked, but I wasn’t entirely thrilled with the result.

So, I looked around my office, found a couple of transparent plastic rulers and a pencil, placed them on the sun paper, and left it by the window.

Isn’t that beautiful? This is a fantastic, hands-on way to understand how we transfer patterns using light. The blue coating on the paper is sensitive to ultraviolet (UV) light from the sun. When you block the light with an object (like a ruler or a pencil), the exposed areas undergo a chemical change.

But the job isn’t finished just by leaving it in the sun. If you look closely after exposure, you might see a faint outline, but you have to dunk the paper into a bowl of water and let it soak for a few minutes to “develop” the image. The water washes away the unreacted chemicals, leaving behind the crisp, white silhouette of your pattern.

The Photolithography Playbook

Let’s connect our sun paper art to actual microfabrication. Photolithography is simply the process of patterning things with light. We went through the steps quickly last time, but I want to break down exactly what we are doing to that silicon wafer.

Imagine you want to make a tiny rectangular strip out of a copper film. You start with a substrate (like a silicon wafer) covered in a thin, continuous layer of copper. This film might be incredibly thin vertically, but horizontally it spans centimeters. Our goal is to chisel that massive sheet down to a really skinny, microscopic pattern.

Step 1: Spin Coating the Photoresist

Just like the sun paper has a blue UV-sensitive layer, we need to coat our wafer with a UV-sensitive polymer called photoresist. We apply this using a technique called spin coating.

We drop a small amount of liquid photoresist onto the center of the wafer, and then use a machine called a spinner to rotate the substrate at thousands of revolutions per minute (RPM).

Check out this animation of the spin coating process: https://makeagif.com/i/c44M0w

The centrifugal force spreads the droplet out into a beautifully uniform, thin layer. Afterward, we usually place the wafer on a hot plate to bake off the solvents. What is left is a semi-solid layer of polymer, somewhat like a thin sheet of plexiglass or a plastic bag, covering your metal film.

Step 2: Exposure in the Clean Room

Next, we bring in our photomask. In my sun paper example, the mask was the physical pencil and rulers. In the lab, it is a glass plate with a high-resolution pattern on it. We align the mask over the wafer and expose it to UV light.

Unlike my office window, real microfabrication never happens out in the sun. The outside world is full of things that will ruin your nanoscale devices: dust, pollen, and bugs. A single speck of dust is like a massive boulder when you are building at the micro-scale. Therefore, all of this happens in a highly controlled environment called a clean room.

To get a great sense of what working in a clean room looks like, I highly recommend watching this video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=udXHWVejDj0

Notice the yellow lighting in the clean room? That is because the photoresist is sensitive to UV and blue light. By filtering those out and only using yellow light, we prevent the photoresist from being accidentally exposed while the researchers are working.

Step 3: Developing and Etching

When the UV light hits the exposed areas of the photoresist, it selectively changes the chemical properties of the polymer—making it either more soluble or less soluble.

Just like dunking the sun paper in water, we dunk our wafer into a special chemical solution called a developer. This washes away the soluble parts of the photoresist, leaving behind a polymer stencil of our desired pattern.

But we aren’t done! We still have a whole hunk of copper film sitting underneath that we need to get rid of. To chisel it down, we use an etching process. We literally bombard the wafer with a beam of heavy ions (like argon). The remaining photoresist acts as a shield, protecting the copper underneath it. The argon ions chip away all the unprotected copper.

Finally, we use another chemical to strip away the leftover photoresist shield, leaving only our beautiful, tiny copper pattern.

Pushing the Limits: How Small Can We Go?

You might be wondering: if we need a photomask to make a tiny pattern, how on earth do we make the tiny pattern on the photomask in the first place? The short answer is that we use a separate, slower process like electron-beam writing to create the master mask. But once you have that mask, you can use it over and over again to mass-produce devices rapidly.

Another great question is: why are we so particular about using UV light?

Light behaves as an electromagnetic wave, with an electric field oscillating up and down. The distance between the peaks of these waves is called the wavelength.

The wavelength of UV light is tiny—less than 300 nanometers. For state-of-the-art microfabrication today, engineers use extreme UV light with wavelengths down to about 13 nanometers!

This matters because the absolute smallest feature you can pattern with photolithography is fundamentally restricted by the wavelength of the light you are using. This restriction is known as the diffraction limit. Because light is a wave, it tends to spread out (diffract) when it passes through a small opening, blurring the edges of your pattern.

We can estimate the smallest possible device pattern we can make using a straightforward relationship:

\begin{align*} \text{Minimum Feature Size} &\approx \frac{\text{Wavelength of Light}}{\text{Numerical Aperture}} \end{align*}

Let’s break that down. The numerator is the wavelength of the light. The smaller the wavelength, the smaller the feature you can print. The denominator, the Numerical Aperture (often abbreviated as NA), is a number that describes the light-gathering ability of the lenses and optics in the system. It is usually a number a little bit less than 1.5.

So, if you want to build smaller transistors to make faster computers, your main strategy is to find a way to use light with a smaller wavelength. We will talk a lot more about the diffraction limit next week.
